sentences.text: The single known species within this genus is named Zhongornis haoae.
Its fossilized remains form a fairly complete skeleton measuring about eight centimeters in length.
Soft tissue traces show feather impressions on the right hand and likely tail feathers near the left foot.
This creature possessed a beaked mouth that lacked any teeth.
It had a proportionately short tail consisting of thirteen vertebrae and no pygostyle.
The third finger contains only two phalangeal bones, a feature shared with Enantiornithes and advanced avialans.
Gao and colleagues described this animal in 2008 based on finds from the Yixian Formation in Lingyuan City, China.
The specimen is currently kept in the collection of the Dalian Natural History Museum.
This fossil offers key anatomical evidence for the evolutionary shift from primitive basal Avialae with long tails to advanced avialans with fused tails.
Zhongornis has only thirteen caudal vertebrae, which is significantly fewer than the twenty-two found in Archaeopteryx.
Although the vertebral centra are not fused, the last four form a continuous lateral flange, implying the specimen had an incipient pygostyle.
Other phylogenetic analyses reject the hypothesis that Zhongornis is a scansoriopterygid, instead placing it as a primitive relative of pygostylians or a close relative of Confuciusornis.
Some researchers consider the scansoriopterygid hypothesis invalid because Zhongornis differs strongly from that group in many traits it shares with birds.
Zhongornis lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, approximately 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
